clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive deficiency of the brush-border enzyme complex sucrase-isomaltase, impairing digestion of sucrose and, to a variable degree, the alpha-1,6-linked limit dextrins derived from starch.
Symptoms characteristically begin when sucrose- and starch-containing foods are introduced at weaning (fruit, juices, cereals) rather than in the exclusively milk-fed neonate.
Osmotic, watery, acidic diarrhoea with abdominal distension, borborygmi, flatulence and colic, and in infants perianal excoriation and weight faltering.
Lactose is typically well tolerated because lactase activity is preserved, distinguishing it from generalised mucosal disaccharidase loss.
Duodenal biopsy disaccharidase assay is the reference standard, showing absent or markedly reduced sucrase with variable isomaltase activity and preserved lactase.
Sucrose breath testing and a monitored trial of sucrose and starch exclusion support the diagnosis, which is confirmed by SI gene sequencing.
Oral enzyme substitution with sacrosidase (a yeast-derived sucrase) allows liberalisation of dietary sucrose, and starch tolerance often improves with age.
Increasingly recognised in older children and adults with functional-type bloating and diarrhoea, where it is frequently mislabelled as irritable bowel syndrome.
reference.pathophysiology: Sucrase-isomaltase is a heavily glycosylated, membrane-anchored disaccharidase expressed on the apical brush border of small-intestinal enterocytes, synthesised as a single polypeptide that is proteolytically processed into sucrase and isomaltase subunits. The complex hydrolyses sucrose into glucose and fructose and also cleaves the alpha-1,6 and some alpha-1,4 glucosidic bonds of starch-derived limit dextrins, complementing maltase-glucoamylase. Biallelic pathogenic variants in the SI gene disrupt enzyme folding, intracellular transport, catalytic function or brush-border targeting, producing several phenotypic classes with differing residual sucrase and isomaltase activity. Undigested sucrose and dextrins remain in the lumen and exert an osmotic load that draws water into the bowel; colonic bacterial fermentation then generates short-chain fatty acids, hydrogen, methane and carbon dioxide, producing acidic stools, gaseous distension and osmotic diarrhoea. Symptom severity varies with the amount and type of carbohydrate ingested, gastric emptying, small-bowel transit and the compensatory fermentative and absorptive capacity of the colon, the last of which tends to increase with age and underlies the clinical improvement often seen over time.
additionalDifferentials: Toddler's diarrhoea (chronic non-specific diarrhoea of childhood)
Irritable bowel syndrome in older children and adults
additionalInvestigations: Small-bowel (duodenal) biopsy with quantitative disaccharidase assay
Sucrose hydrogen and methane breath testing
Stool pH and reducing substances following a sucrose load
Molecular genetic testing of the SI gene
Monitored trial of dietary sucrose and starch exclusion with a symptom diary
Coeliac serology with total IgA to exclude coexisting enteropathy
Faecal studies to exclude persistent enteric infection where relevant
redFlags: Weight faltering or failure to thrive in an infant with chronic diarrhoea
Dehydration and electrolyte disturbance during intercurrent illness
Severe perianal excoriation and pain from acidic stools
Persistent symptoms despite apparent dietary adherence, suggesting hidden carbohydrate or an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent with dietary modification and, where needed, oral enzyme substitution, and many patients tolerate increasing amounts of starch and sucrose as they grow and colonic adaptation develops. Growth and nutrition normalise once the offending carbohydrates are controlled.
pitfalls: Attributing symptoms to toddler's diarrhoea, functional bloating or irritable bowel syndrome and overlooking the diagnosis
Falsely negative breath tests owing to recent antibiotics or a non-hydrogen-producing (methanogenic) microbiome
Improper handling of biopsy specimens giving spuriously low disaccharidase activity
Assuming preserved lactose tolerance excludes a disaccharidase disorder
